<reason>A built a clean, sustained asymmetry argument (irreversibility of true gene drives vs. every other tested technology) and used it to pressure B's case at three critical junctures: (1) B's "staged ladder" defense of starting with self-limiting/marked constructs let A argue that PRO was quietly defending a different, reversible technology while the resolution's actual subject—self-propagating drives—stayed deferred to an unspecified future; (2) A's vaccine/insecticide disanalogy (you can halt a bad vaccine trial, but not a spreading genetic element) directly rebutted B's capacity analogy; (3) A exposed B's "neighbor notification" language as discretionary ("should reroute," not "must"), turning B's own wording into an admission that consent wasn't really being offered to third countries. B's closing charge that A's evidentiary bar creates an unbreakable circularity (a brake can't be validated without real-world release) was a fair point, but A had already partially preempted it by locating brake-testing within the self-limiting stage, and B never cleanly resolved whether their staged approach actually defends the resolution's core ask (permitting true drive trials now) or merely postpones it. B's case retained real force — the urgency of malaria deaths, the double standard on insecticide monitoring, and the veto-vs-sovereignty framing — but these points were answered rather than left to dominate, whereas A's central asymmetry point was never squarely dismantled. Both sides handled the Pressure Questions and A1/A2 format correctly, but A's answers advanced its case while B's answers mostly reasserted prior claims.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's [A2.1]/[A4.6] sequence — catching B's "self-limiting/marked constructs" defense and reframing it as a concession that the resolution's actual subject (self-propagating drives) remains undefended until later, unspecified conditions — was the most damaging and least fully answered exchange of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
